questions.q: In the lab's 4-asset problem, what is the naive 'pick the highest returns' choice, and what is the true brute-force optimum?
options: Naive pick is (1,1,0,0) with F=-0.0800; true optimum is (1,0,0,1) with F=-0.0850
Naive pick is (1,0,0,1) with F=-0.0850; true optimum is (1,1,0,0) with F=-0.0800
Both the naive pick and true optimum are (1,1,0,0)
The true optimum is (0,0,1,1), which also happens to be the naive pick
questions.explain: Picking the two highest-return assets gives x=(1,1,0,0) with F=-0.0800, but brute-force checking all 16 combinations reveals x=(1,0,0,1) achieves a lower (better) F=-0.0850, despite asset 4 having the lowest individual return.

questions.q: Why does x = (1,0,0,1) beat the naive pick x = (1,1,0,0) in this lab, despite asset 4 having the weakest individual return?
options: Assets 1 and 4 have zero covariance (Sigma_14 = 0.00), so pairing them produces a much lower combined risk term (0.075 vs 0.130), which outweighs asset 4's lower individual return under the given risk aversion
Asset 4 actually has the highest return in the dataset, making this not surprising at all
The penalty term favors x=(1,0,0,1) specifically regardless of risk or return
Covariance has no effect on which combination wins; only individual returns matter
questions.explain: Because Sigma_14 = 0.00 means assets 1 and 4 move independently, the risk term for (1,0,0,1) is much lower (0.075) than for (1,1,0,0) (0.130), and this risk reduction is large enough to overcome asset 4's weaker return under the lesson's risk-aversion setting.

questions.q: Why is brute-force checking all 16 combinations feasible in this lab but not for a real-world portfolio problem?
options: 2^n grows combinatorially -- 16 combinations for n=4 is trivial, but real portfolios with hundreds of assets produce combination counts far beyond any brute-force search, motivating heuristic methods like QAOA
Brute-force search is always feasible regardless of problem size
Real portfolios never have more than 4 assets in practice
Covariance matrices cannot be computed for more than 4 assets
questions.explain: This directly echoes Lesson 1: 2^n combinations is trivial at n=4 (16) but becomes intractable at real portfolio scale, which is exactly why QAOA and other heuristics (rather than brute force) are needed for realistically sized problems.

questions.q: What is the full end-to-end pipeline this lab's closing checklist traces, connecting back through the whole course?
options: Real problem -> QUBO -> Ising Hamiltonian (via s=1-2x) -> Pauli-Z cost Hamiltonian -> QAOA circuit -> classically optimized, approximation-ratio-scored result
Real problem -> VQE ansatz -> molecular ground state energy -> final answer, with no QUBO involved
QUBO -> real problem -> Ising Hamiltonian -> amplitude estimation -> classical Monte Carlo
Pauli-Z cost Hamiltonian -> real problem -> QUBO -> Ising Hamiltonian, in that specific reverse order
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly traces: real-world problem -> QUBO (Lesson 15) -> Ising Hamiltonian via the s=1-2x substitution (Lesson 3) -> Pauli-Z cost Hamiltonian (Lesson 7) -> QAOA circuit (Lesson 6) -> classically optimized result scored by approximation ratio (Lesson 9).
